processing: Mostly green tea, either flat and straight in the top Cuifeng style or curled, pearl- and needle-shaped in everyday grades. A black tea is also made under the same name.
harvest_season: Spring is the usual prized picking, as with other Guizhou greens; the Cuifeng style needs tender early leaf.
appearance_dry: Top green grades are flat, straight, smooth and emerald; everyday grades are curled or pearled and glossy green.
appearance_liquor: Clear, tender green for the green teas; bright red for the black tea.
appearance_wet: Tender, even and bright green in the green teas; fine and bud-rich in the black.
taste_profile: Greens are fresh and mellow with a lasting tender-leaf aroma and sweet aftertaste. The black tea is sweet and mellow, with a sweet scent and a slight floral note.

brewing.notes: This is for the green teas. Brew the black version hotter, around 90 to 95 C.

vintage_note: Green grades are sold as the current year's harvest, with spring lots as the usual premium, as with most Chinese greens. The black tea keeps longer but is also normally sold as recent production, not by vintage.
description:
Fanjingshan tea is the regional name for tea from the Fanjing Mountain area of Tongren in northeast Guizhou, with Yinjiang county as its home. It is an appellation rather than one recipe, covering seven counties and both green and black teas.

The best-known form is Cuifeng, a flat, straight, emerald green tea in the same general family of shape as Long Jing. Everyday green grades are curled, pearled or needle-shaped, and there is also a fine, gold-flecked black tea. Provincial standards exist for Cuifeng and for the area's green tea.

The flat greens are fresh and mellow with a tender-leaf smell and a sweet finish. Flat leaf gives up its flavour quickly, so short steeps in water a little under boiling work best. The black tea is sweet and soft, with a slight floral lift.

Because the name covers so much, read the label closely: green or black, Cuifeng or everyday grade, and which season. Tuanlong village is the historic heart, and tea sold with that link deserves a question about what it actually means.
history:
Local accounts begin with a man named Chai bringing tea seed to Tuanlong in 1369. Merchants from Hunan and Sichuan settled in the area from 1409 and set up tea bases for trade. In 1411 Tuanlong tea is said to have been sent to the court and named a tribute tea. Tea in the area itself is sometimes traced back to the 11th century, but that is much less certain.

The tea grew on its own until about 1986. From 1987 Yinjiang began planting in a planned way and treating tea as a pillar industry, and after 2007 it moved toward branded, higher-grade production.

The tea was named a Guizhou famous tea in 2006 and 2007, and national agricultural geographical indication registration followed on 2 November 2016.
